comments.text: Lines 10-28: `*FX200,3`, which makes BREAK clear memory and also turns the ESCAPE key off (the MOS's &0258 = 3), then MODE 7, the cursor off, paged mode off and CLS (VDU 15,12). Nothing in this program leads anywhere else: it never CHAINs the menu, so once the story is running only BREAK, which clears memory, or SHIFT-BREAK, which boots the disc again, gets the player out.

Line 30, the title page: two yellow boxes (PROCbox), the first round `4MATION Educational Resources` and `THE FLOWERS OF CRYSTAL STORY` in double height, blue on a yellow band (the red text code before it is overridden at once by blue, &84); the second round `To start and to page the story` and `press < S > space`, the S red on yellow (live).

Lines 45-60, the story itself. The space bar starts it and clears the screen. Each page is seven DATA items: an item is printed twice in double height (CHR$141), at the left of row 24 each time, and the PRINTs scroll the screen up, so each line enters from the bottom and every line of text takes three rows, one of them blank (live). An item `*` prints nothing. After the seven: a pause of 0.8 seconds (TIME), the keyboard buffer emptied (`*FX15,0`) so that a key pressed early is not taken, and a wait for the space bar. The page that reads the `*` items of line 620 is the last; its space bar RUNs the program again, back to the title page.

PROCbox(a,b,x,ln), lines 90-96: a box of yellow teletext graphics (&93) from row a to row b, its left edge at column x and its inside ln wide: graphics characters <, l, - and . at the corners, a thin line of commas along the top and bottom, the sides 5 and j with white text (&87) between, TAB(ln) clearing the inside. The worksheet program has the same procedure.

Lines 100-112, DATA, the story's first items: `FLOWERS OF CRYSTAL` in yellow on a red band, then Rumala, a very old and very wise woman on a far-off world, alone but never lonely among the wild creatures she knew and loved; a row of cyan stars (&86) marks the end of the passage. Then a blue bleeper hops onto her hand.

Lines 115-130, DATA: the bleeper, frightened, tells Rumala, who speaks every creature's language, that a terrible monster is tearing up the trees and clawing holes in the earth; she packs an old cloth bag and sets off to see it.

Lines 140-150, DATA: after a row of magenta stars (&85), the monster turns out to be a machine clearing the ground for hotels, cafés and shops; tourists from many worlds come for Crystal's forests, lakes and streams, and each day more of the planet disappears under glass and concrete.

Lines 160-190, DATA: after a row of yellow stars, the Crystal Flower, whose roots make a chemical the Blids hate. The Blids, ugly, slimy, worm-like creatures, live in deep burrows and dare not come near the surface for fear of the flower; the tourists love to pick it, and the important people are too busy making money to listen to Rumala's warnings.

Lines 200-240, DATA: after a row of green stars, Mr. Grubble, the richest and probably the fattest man on Crystal, who loves bubble gum: he built a bubble gum factory and bought the only forest whose sap makes gum that blows big bubbles.

Lines 250-260, DATA: after a row of red stars, the bubble-blowing contest beside The Hole, a gigantic fenced pit, and after the final of the Under-Twelves Mixed Doubles a competition to spit old gum into it from the greatest distance.

Lines 270-290, DATA: every piece of gum that falls into The Hole brings squeaking and hissing from the depths: the Blids are at the bottom, waiting for it. Grubble sees his fortune: he will sell gum to the Blids for the precious metals in the rocks below.

Lines 300-330, DATA: after a row of cyan stars, Rumala, long before Grubble was born, plans the planet's survival and gathers with her magic the items that may one day save it, listed: 1. a bag of soil from many parts of the planet, 2. a sack of fertiliser of secret ingredients, 3. a bottle of magic spell water, 4. an enchanted gold pot. Empty items leave blank lines around the list.

Lines 340-350, DATA: she hides the treasures under ancient spells, takes one Crystal Flower to a secret place and surrounds it with nightmares and horrors; the place becomes known as the Danger Area, and the Government of Crystal lets no-one go there.

Lines 360-380, DATA: only the odd child strays into the forbidden zone, and comes running out with stories of fearful storms and bright blue blob-like creatures falling from the clouds; Rumala writes a message in the skies to a man who will not be born until long after her death.

Lines 390-410, DATA: after a row of magenta stars, years later, Grubble's troubles begin: the Crystal Flowers kill the Blids that come up for their gum, so he opens flower shops all over the planet to be rid of the flowers.
Lines 420-430, DATA: as the flowers disappear, more Blids reach the surface and their tunnels make the ground unsafe: children fall into cracks, homes crumble and whole towns are abandoned as ruins.

Lines 440-480, DATA: after a row of yellow stars, the ruins are called Grubble-rubble and everyone hates Grubble; he hires the toughest, meanest people he can find as bodyguards, Grubble's Grabbers, who roam the world grabbing anyone who looks as if they do not like him. No tourists come, and Crystal grows poor.

Lines 490-510, DATA: after a row of green stars, little Jim, thought strange by his family and bonkers by his few friends, keeps asking about the writing in the sky, which only he can see: Rumala made her words visible to a special person like him.

Lines 520-530, DATA: Jim's ideas for dealing with Grubble and the Blids, such as filling their holes with extra-hard concrete, given up as too cruel and because his parents thought a train set a better birthday present than a concrete mixer; and his claim that a Crystal Flower is hidden somewhere, though the plant is taught at school to be extinct.

Lines 540-550, DATA: after a row of red stars, the Government of Crystal gives Jim the job of saving the world. The writing in the sky has told him that magical items are hidden around the planet, which no Crystallian could ever find.

Lines 560-580, DATA: so Jim must find someone from a world on the other side of the galaxy, and builds a vast computer in a windowless, top-secret building, The Centre, where part 1 begins; he becomes Super Jim. `Grubble, of course, had other ideas.` A last row of stars flashes (&88, blue).
Lines 600-615, DATA: the closing words in yellow, to the visitor from planet Earth, wishing them success in finding the last Flower of Crystal, then `< S >` and `to begin again`.
Line 620, DATA: seven `*` items, the end of the story. Line 45 skips them, and line 60 ends its REPEAT on them and RUNs the program again.

The end of the program, one byte short: the file stops after this &0D, and the &FF that should follow it is outside the file, so whether BASIC finds the end depends on what memory held at &49F4 before the load (orientation.md, "STORY is one byte short").
